rewrites.summary: North Korea is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely: same-sex conduct is not named in the Criminal Code, but Article 193 prohibits “decadent culture,” and broad obscene-activities provisions give the authorities unlimited discretion, and reported incidents of criminalisation and even execution for homosexuality exist. Gender identity does not exist in public life, visitors travel under constant escort and surveillance in the world's most totalitarian system, and any nonconforming presentation or discovered digital material risks detention, with no recorded protection or recognition of gender identity to offset that exposure.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: Adjacent policy flux: new laws in the decade after the UN Commission of Inquiry's 2014 report, including the Pyongyang Cultural Protection Act, tightened control over expression and digital material, and the official record shows the government news agency rejecting the inquiry's human-rights report as a political fabrication and personally attacking one of its commissioners as “a disgusting old lecher with a 40-odd-year-long career of homosexuality” — official-record evidence of regime hostility toward homosexuality even while the regime denies its existence. No neighbour comparisons or domestic litigation flux are recorded in the sources; the international inquiry process is the only adjacent mechanism on the record.
rewrites.localsOnly:
Resident-facing facts: sex-marker changes on birth certificates or citizen cards are technically possible only “under unavoidable circumstances” — application to the People's Security Agency plus a government forensic medical evaluation — and in practice require surgical intervention; no law explicitly bans gender-affirming care, but the under-resourced health system makes hormones and surgery effectively inaccessible.

Civil society has no registration route for LGBTI organisations, and resident experience is documented by an openly gay defector's 2017 autobiography and by a broadcaster's profile of a novelist who defected in the late 1990s and was forcibly outed as the first publicly known gay defector; the profile documents how a collective-over-individual regime forces sexual minorities into silent self-suppression.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: No source in this record covers visa or border-document screening of foreign trans visitors, and no marriage or partner-travel recognition fact for trans visitors is recorded anywhere in the sources — the criminal-code and surveillance profile is the entire documented visitor picture. One source records no documented violence against LGBTIQ people, by the government or by other actors, which sits in tension with the reported criminalisation and even execution incidents in the current summary; neither side is independently verified. Data scarcity reflects totalitarian control, and traveler surveillance is universal.

blindSourceSummaries: An international advocacy organisation's country page (updated 12 Mar 2026): the criminal code (1950, revised 2009) appears to contain no penalty for consensual same-sex acts, but one article bans the import, keeping or distribution of 'decadent culture' including sexual recordings and another bans collective 'obscene activities'; the official news agency denied homosexuality's existence in 2014; an openly gay defector published an autobiography in 2017; no documented violence against LGBTIQ people by the government or by other actors is recorded, and no registration route exists for LGBTI organisations.

A legal-information overview: sex-marker changes on birth certificates or citizen cards are technically possible under 'unavoidable circumstances' — application to a security agency plus a government forensic medical evaluation, in practice requiring surgical intervention; no law explicitly bans gender-affirming care, but the under-resourced health system makes hormones and surgery effectively inaccessible.

A broadcaster's feature in the local language (10 Oct 2024): in the decade after an international human-rights inquiry's report, new laws including a cultural protection act tightened control; it profiles a novelist who defected in the late 1990s and was forcibly outed, described as the first publicly known gay defector, and documents how the regime forces sexual minorities into silent self-suppression and frames LGBT life as a human-rights abuse.
A national government human-rights report (2022): official assessment — the regime's pervasive abuses leave no space for LGBT life even though no specific law criminalises same-sex conduct.
A national government human-rights report (2020): official assessment — no reliable information on LGBT persons exists, and the regime's repression of all civil society is the dominant reality.

A news report (Apr 2017): a defector's first-person account of the place of homosexuality in the country's society and of its punishment, and of a life in which the person could not even dream openly.

The official news agency's commentary (22 Apr 2014): the agency rejects an international human-rights inquiry's report on the country as a political fabrication and personally attacks one of the inquiry's commissioners with a slur about a decades-long record of homosexuality — official-record evidence of regime hostility toward homosexuality even while its existence is denied.
